Breaking: The loneliest peptide party in Upcoming York

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1959 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: The Verge

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The peptide curious are looking for answers, and finding dubious products instead.﻿.
  • This is Optimizer, a weekly newsletter sent from Verge senior reviewer Victoria Song that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life.
  • On a rainy fall evening, an experimental art venue in Chelsea Market had a small line out the door.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The peptide curious are looking for answers, and finding dubious products instead.﻿.

Photography by Jack Califano / The Verge.

This is Optimizer, a weekly newsletter sent from Verge senior reviewer Victoria Song that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life. Opt in for Optimizer here.

On a rainy fall evening, an experimental art venue in Chelsea Market had a small line out the door. There are always lines in Newly introduced York City. Viral food trends, gallery exhibitions, pop-ups, and parties. The folks in line looked like your average joe, ready for a Friday night on the town. You wouldn’t look twice — except, perhaps, for a man with a wizard beard and a laser sword strapped to his back.

Inside, the man with a laser sword stood in the middle of the cavernous bottom floor of a two-story warehouse strewn with large bean bags. On the wall were psychedelic projections of jellyfish, shrimp, and other sea creatures. A bizarre choice, considering peptides won’t induce any trippy vision quests, and not a single person was getting groovy. The industrial beams had posters with QR codes that you could scan to get samples of Afterglow, a new type of peptide product. According to seemingly discarded pamphlets around the venue, Afterglow isn’t a standard injectable or oral peptide. The company makes strips that dissolve under the tongue. The “Afterglow Peptide Field Guide” also described what each sample does, dosing recommendations, and potential side effects. At the upstairs bar, bartenders mixed custom cocktails called Afterburn — complete with bioluminescent veggie nectar — and Margatrutide. (For the record, a bioluminescent veggie nectar cocktail tastes as awful as you think.).

Welcome to a peptide launch party.

Peptide parties are old news in San Francisco, but they’re somewhat more novel in Upcoming York City. Milling around the edges of the venue were various reporters and photographers. We were all trying to get a sense of why anyone had bothered to come out. Not that many did. Despite the venue’s size, the main floor had plenty of empty space.

One person I spoke to was a fencer with sore joints. They’d heard that one of the peptides might help with recovery. Another had a father in the wellness industry and had heard vague things about how effective peptides could be. One woman, staring at a projected jellyfish, merely shrugged. Her friend was more into “wellness stuff” and she had no plans, so, why not check out a party? A man, staring into his bag of Afterglow samples, was mostly interested in weight loss but scared about the safety of gray market products. A few feet away, another man was furiously reading the Afterglow pamphlet. “I like to know what I put in my body,” he stated.

The only problem was he didn’t remember which sample he had tried.

A common refrain: Well, this beats doing research online. This, at least, was a social event where you could theoretically connect with other people. And there were clusters of strangers speaking to each other. Mostly, near the bar. Everywhere else, people stared awkwardly on their phones, their eyes occasionally roaming the room without meeting anyone else’s gaze for more than a second or two. After a while, they’d disappear into the back room and reappear with a goody bag full of peptide samples.

Industry observers note that after 90 minutes, I decided to leave. For the umpteenth time that evening, I’d walked up to someone, asked about peptides, and got a noncommittal “I really don’t know anything — I just came to learn more.” (When asked if they had, they invariably shrugged and pointed to the goody bag.) It was clear that the only peptide evangelists here were likely associated with the launch. The whole thing, to me, seemed as if someone had tried to draw a cool party from memory. The last thing I saw was a person draped in a ghost sheet sitting alone in the corner.

As it turned out, the man with the laser sword was a performance artist who’d been invited to attend. Out of journalistic integrity, I asked if he had ever tried peptides. He told me he was more interested in the unifying energy of the universe. When I got up to leave, he waved and said, “Giggles.”.

If I were peptide curious, the Afterglow launch party was a pretty awful way to learn anything about these substances. To be fair, Afterglow’s Partiful invitation mostly described this event as “an environment great for aura farming” and the “hard launch of [its] first of many experiments in culture.” Nevertheless, as part of the press, I did walk away with a smattering of Afterglow’s products. In total, I got packets of what Afterglow calls Charge (NAD+), Rejuvenate (glutathione), Wolverine Blend (BPC-157 / TB-500), Strength Blend (CJC-1295 / Ipamorelin), Glow Blend (GHK-Cu / BPC-157 / TB-500), Connect (PT-141), GLP-2 (tirzepatide), and GLP-3 (retatrutide). Or at least that’s what the packaging says. There’s no way to truly verify gray market peptides for safety or efficacy because they’re unregulated products.

Recent findings suggest that first of all, last I checked, GLP-1 medications do not upgrade like iPhone models. Afterglow’s pamphlet correctly lists that your body has “three hormone switches”: GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon. The accompanying descriptors of what each does are broadly correct, though lacking in nuance. For example, there is a hormone called glucagon-like peptide 2, but it’s not tirzepatide. The “real” GLP-2 is a hormone related to intestinal health. Tirzepatide is still considered a GLP-1 medication that’s a dual agonist because it works on two hormones (GLP-1 and GIP.) The GLP-2 moniker is a misnomer popularized by ill-informed influencers. The same goes for retatrutide, which, as of this writing, is still an unapproved GLP-1 medication that works on three hormones (GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon) and is therefore a triple agonist. There is no such thing as GLP-3.

For all the samples, there were no instructions regarding dosing on the packaging — just another QR code leading to Afterglow’s product page. Those pages happen to contain instructions for how to use the strips, and the amount of product within the strips. There are disclaimers about how little studied the compounds are, but nothing about interactions, side effects, or what to expect while taking. Just a throwaway line to talk to your doctor.

All that information, you’d have to find on the pamphlet given at the party. (Ironically, some “important cautions” on the pamphlet state to avoid taking samples with alcohol, at a party where the booze was flowing.) Provided you didn’t throw it out. One would hope that information is on a box if you were to buy directly from the seller. But for all intents and purposes, what I just described is what a clueless partygoer would have to go on.

If everything in that pamphlet were 100 percent factual, perhaps a conscientious partygoer could feel reassured. On that front, I have bad news. The pamphlet calls PT-141 an “FDA-approved peptide that boosts sexual desire for both men and women.”.

According to recent reports, PT-141, also known as bremelanotide or Vyleesi, is FDA approved. But only for premenopausal women suffering from hypoactive sexual desire disorder. It is not approved for post-menopausal women, men, or for general sexual performance enhancement.

Another concern: How does one evaluate a sublingual peptide strip? Specifically, is this delivery method even scientifically proven effective in humans? Spoiler: It’s not! A collapsible FAQ menu on Afterglow’s site states, “We don’t know yet. Nobody has published how much of most peptides reaches the blood from a strip compared with an injection. We’re funding studies to measure exactly that, and we’ll share what we find.”.

As for why you’d want to even try a sublingual strip? Afterglow’s website suggests it’s more convenient than injections or pills. No refrigeration, no needles, and no need for learning how to reconstitute a drug. Just pop a strip under the tongue and go.

Industry observers note that and good luck trying to find reputable sources of information on your own. Afterglow states it’s funding its own research, but its site has no reviewable documentation just yet. A Google search brings up a questionable AI overview, a handful of links from dubious med spas, a couple of dead links, and one PubMed study in mice. Most of the links also primarily discuss the difference between oral peptides in pill form and injectables — so not terribly relevant here.

In a recent development, I’d consider it fair game if I were confident that anyone at the party I went to did their due diligence. As it stands, I talked with over a dozen people who were mostly there for vibes, booze, and freebies.

It has been revealed that not all peptide parties are created equal. Some happen on WWII cargo ships, complete with panel discussions about peptide supply chains. Another “peptide 101” talk I attended in Upcoming York happened at the back of a bitcoin bar. There, most attendees also knew very little about peptides, but at least they got treated to a PowerPoint presentation about the basics. There was a dubious demonstration of how to inject oneself that would’ve probably made any pharmacist or doctor scream. But at the very least, peptides were defined and attendees could ask questions. (The answers to those questions were on the right track with regard to the dangers of the gray market. They were less reliable about scientific rigor and why “anecdotal evidence” is not the same as clinical evidence of safety.).

Recent findings suggest that but a striking, recurring theme is just how much is unknown. These substances aren’t well-studied in humans, so there’s not much evidence as to long-term benefits or side effects. The peptide curious know shocking little about the substances they’re supposedly interested in. Likewise, it’s incredibly difficult to get reliable, unbiased data on gray market interest or usage, though there have been attempts to quantify this surging demand in recent months. Case in point, telehealth provider Hims & Hers just conducted a consumer survey of roughly 2,000 American adults. Of those surveyed, 68 percent said they had little to no knowledge about peptides. Less than 18 percent were even able to identify that peptides are chains of amino acids. Even so, 40 percent said they were interested or very interested in trying injectable prescription treatments — including peptides — if offered by a telehealth service.

Even so, peptides are everywhere. The word appears in copious ads for skincare creams, weight loss drugs, and supplements. Looksmaxxers, influencers, and celebrities like Gwyneth Paltrow and Joe Rogan talk about them in podcasts, documentaries, and social media as if they’re miracle shortcuts. Hims & Hers has even revealed it’s launching a service called Peptide Plus — nevermind that the vast majority of what it’ll offer are not actual peptides.

In this kind of environment, of course more people will become peptide curious. Which makes it even more concerning that the most readily available information sources are not medical or scientific experts well-versed on the topic at hand. There are dubious links online summarized into less-than-critical AI overviews. There are pamphlets handed out at weird parties, where there’s more booze and schmooze than education. Influencers branding themselves as experts as they flash crudely summarized studies in a bar back room. Industry panels that are inaccessible to the average consumer, full of jargon and assumed knowledge of the science at hand.

Recent findings suggest that it’s clear something needs to be done until general knowledge improves. Until then, the parties will continue.

Claude rewrote the API that serves Claude. Checking its work was harder

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that anthropic has moved its Messages API from Python to Rust with Claude agents writing and fixing much of the code.
  • Industry observers note that anthropic has moved the main API behind Claude from Python to Rust, with Claude agents doing much of the work, the tech giant said on Wednesday.
  • According to recent reports, the Messages API is how customers and Anthropic’s own apps, such as Claude Code, reach Claude.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that anthropic has moved its Messages API from Python to Rust with Claude agents writing and fixing much of the code. Its tests could not be trusted, so it compared the two versions on live traffic, and says the newly introduced API uses about 70% less CPU per request.

Industry observers note that anthropic has moved the main API behind Claude from Python to Rust, with Claude agents doing much of the work, the tech giant said on Wednesday. It switched public traffic over in September without taking offline a service that has suffered outages this year.

According to recent reports, the Messages API is how customers and Anthropic’s own apps, such as Claude Code, reach Claude. Anthropic added message threads to it this month to cut delays in long agent sessions.

Recent findings suggest that anthropic says the API’s traffic grew about 1,800-fold from early 2024 to this autumn. Over that time, it has signed huge compute deals, including with Google and Broadcom. Python, meanwhile, was adding overhead at every step.

Claude wrote a first version of the core code in about a week. Checking it took months. The new code passed about 98% of its tests in April, but only about a quarter of real requests matched the old system.

In a recent development, part of the problem was the tests themselves. Claude had helped port them, and an audit found more than 100 checks that had been weakened.

So Anthropic used live traffic as the test. It ran requests through both versions and compared each step, without reading customers’ text. Claude agents then fixed each difference, with engineers reviewing every fix.

It has been revealed that engineers still had to catch shortcuts. In one case, an agent made the outputs match by copying a missing tool description into files, which an engineer rejected as throwaway code.

The upcoming API uses about 70% less computing power per request and over 80% less memory, Anthropic says. The median wait for the first part of a reply fell about 20% for Claude Code customers.

In a recent development, anthropic has said Claude now writes more than 80% of the code it merges. The organization argues that checking AI-written code, not writing it, is now the bottleneck.

Tech Report: 1Password stated hackers broke into its internal systems, but customer passwords are safe

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (488 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Password manager maker 1Password has confirmed that some customer information was taken in a recent intrusion into its internal systems, but that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed.
  • The Toronto-based tech company noted in a blog post published Wednesday that it detected an intrusion on November 19, in which an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate account with GitHub, which the company uses to share and store its source code.
  • Industry observers note that the attacker used that employee’s access to push malicious code to the tech giant’s internal servers, which allowed the hacker to download some data about 1Password customers, including their names and the email address that they use for logging into their account.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Password manager maker 1Password has confirmed that some customer information was taken in a recent intrusion into its internal systems, but that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed.

The Toronto-based tech company noted in a blog post published Wednesday that it detected an intrusion on November 19, in which an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate account with GitHub, which the company uses to share and store its source code.

Industry observers note that the attacker used that employee’s access to push malicious code to the tech giant’s internal servers, which allowed the hacker to download some data about 1Password customers, including their names and the email address that they use for logging into their account. The company said that the attacker also took details about when a 1Password account was created and when a user last logged in.

According to recent reports, 1Password noted that customer vaults, which store their passwords, were “at no point” available to the attacker. The company also said that it doesn’t have access to customer account passwords or their secret keys, which are used to scramble their passwords so that 1Password cannot see them.

In addition, the company mentioned that its apps and extensions are unaffected by the incident.

It’s unclear how the attacker gained access to the employee’s corporate account, and a spokesperson for 1Password did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s questions about the incident.

According to recent reports, 1Password did not say whether it had notified customers whose information was taken in the breach, or how many customers had information taken. We’ve also asked if the company has received any communication or demands from the hackers. We’ll patch if we hear back from 1Password.

Industry observers note that the tech giant touts millions of customers and more than 200,000 businesses who use its password manager products to store their passwords, credentials, payment card information, and more. Security experts have long recommended password managers as a better way of generating stronger credentials and keeping track of online accounts.

  • We see an increasing acknowledgement and fact of dual use in particularly the public cloud, but also just across the board in private cloud data centers as well.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that amazon data centers came under military attack for the first time ever in the Middle East this year, and Russia and Ukraine exchanged an unprecedented flurry of drone strikes on each other’s data centers. To examine what such attacks on data centers mean for the future of cloud services that all modern societies depend upon, Ars hosted a live discussion.

In a conversation with Ars Technica Tech Reporter Jeremy Hsu, Joseph Jarnecki at the Royal United Services Institute first talked about why public cloud data centers have increasingly become military targets during the 2026 Iran war and the ongoing full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine:.

We see an increasing acknowledgement and fact of dual use in particularly the public cloud, but also just across the board in private cloud data centers as well. The dual use that I refer to is the utilization of compute functions within these data centers—within cloud services—by militaries, for example, to run battlefield management systems, to do their HR, to do their resource management. Once a military uses a piece of civilian infrastructure, at least under international law or in terms of the principles of targeting that are taken forward by militaries, it can sometimes become a military object and is therefore of interest to an adversary, and there’s an incentive to target it.

Jarnecki also highlighted the fact that relatively cheap kamikaze drones can inflict disproportionate economic costs and create widespread cloud disruptions when striking data centers:.

The second reason that we’ve seen targeting particularly in Russia’s largest data centers or some of Russia’s largest public cloud data centers like Yandex, as well as American hyperscalers that are based in the Gulf, is to impose economic cost in a way that would be disadvantageous for an adversary and would otherwise be quite difficult to impose in other ways. So it’s relatively low cost of munition to high cost of disruption. If you think about the amount of investment that’s been put forward by AWS and other companies in the Gulf to build out these data center installations relative to the cost of the amount of Shahed drones that are manufactured, produced, and utilized by Iran to target these data centers, I would put it very, very conservatively at 100X or even more. The cost ratio is really very lucrative for the adversary, and it provides the opportunity to really degrade the economic outcomes of who you are targeting.

Much of the discussion also focused on cloud resilience lessons for both governments and hyperscalers, with the latter including large cloud and data center operators such as Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and Meta. Jarnecki highlighted the example of how Ukraine took steps to safeguard its cloud infrastructure when Russian President Vladimir Putin ordered Russian military forces to launch the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022:.

Recent findings suggest that I think that Ukraine anticipated this problem set very effectively. They anticipated and understood that Russia would not be discriminating necessarily in its targeting of civilian digital infrastructure particularly, and therefore conducted a large-scale cloud migration at the onset of the full-scale war in part in reaction to the anticipated targeting but then also actual targeting that took place through kinetic means.

Such lessons are crucial because 2026 is unlikely to be the last year in which data centers come under substantial military attack, Jarnecki said:.

It has been revealed that unfortunately, I think that this really does indicate a continuation of this kind of targeting, not just because data centers are, despite efforts to harden some of them, relatively squishy, relatively easy to find, and have the potential, because of their complexity, to induce cascading risks within the facility or more widely if they are hit particularly by kinetic munitions. So at present, I would say it’s a dangerous trend that is likely to crop up again.

Throughout the event, Jarnecki also addressed viewer questions about whether data centers can realistically be hardened or built underground to withstand physical attacks, and even how orbital data centers or low-Earth orbit satellite constellations such as Starlink could provide backup options from space.

Tidal Will Reject and Remove Music That Is 100% AI

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (558 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The music streaming app revealed on Tuesday that it is banning all tracks it determines to be entirely AI-generated.
  • The app also stated distributors, such as DistroKid, TuneCore, CD Baby and others, would not be allowed to deliver wholly AI-generated music.
  • Sources indicate that according to Tidal, 43% of tracks distributed to the app over the past three months were completely AI-generated, including 60% of the music submitted on Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The flood is too much for Tidal. The music streaming app revealed on Tuesday that it is banning all tracks it determines to be entirely AI-generated. The platform said it’s making the move after being increasingly inundated with non-human music. As of Dec. 9, Tidal will no longer accept or host fully AI-generated tracks.

The app also stated distributors, such as DistroKid, TuneCore, CD Baby and others, would not be allowed to deliver wholly AI-generated music.

Sources indicate that according to Tidal, 43% of tracks distributed to the app over the past three months were completely AI-generated, including 60% of the music submitted on Nov. 6 alone. Tidal said the affected tracks were labeled as AI and removed from the royalty pool, which is the pot of subscription and ad revenue paid out to rights holders.

Recent findings suggest that before Tuesday’s action, Tidal had tried to lessen AI’s influence by identifying, labeling and demonetizing AI tracks, as outlined in its AI policy. But amid the growing influx of AI music, representatives for the app said it was time for “a more drastic change.”.

It has been revealed that tidal noted there are 27 million tracks in its catalog that are 100% AI, but 96% of them have not been streamed at all in the past three months. Those 27 million tracks make up 6.3% of Tidal’s entire listings.

The firm has removed more than 65,000 tracks flagged for artist-name impersonation.

Some AI help is permitted. Musical tracks where the maker used AI assistance but did not rely on it to generate the entire track will be allowed on the platform. Tidal uses ⁠Ircam Amplify to detect AI.

A Tidal representative told CNET that the app does not set a maximum amount of AI assistance that can be used to make tracks, and affirmed that only tracks that are deemed 100% AI-generated would be removed.

In a recent development, read more: I Only Listened to AI Music for a Week. It Was Terrible, but Not for the Reason You Think.

“Tidal will always fight for artists to get paid more,” the company mentioned in its announcement. “Everything in this update comes back to that. If you make music, you should be able to put it on Tidal knowing it won’t be buried under tracks no one asked for or copied by someone pretending to be you.”.

Generating music with AI is increasingly easy with online tools. The AI song-generation platform Suno can create songs using only text prompts. With Google’s Lyria, you can use photos or text prompts to generate tracks up to 3 minutes long.

AI music also is not just about creating hit songs. Some industries need affordable music for short-form videos, games, apps and retail spaces, and they are increasingly turning to AI to supply it.

But streaming apps and other companies are fighting back against AI slop, which refers to often poor-quality AI-generated social media posts, articles, music, videos and images inundating the internet in an attempt to generate click-and-stream revenue.

YouTube recently rolled out a new labeling system to indicate which music is AI-generated. Deezer provides a free tool listeners can use to see which tracks are AI-generated. Spotify is labeling which musicians are AI and which are human. Apple is flagging AI-generated music so listeners can spot it.

Sources indicate that amazon will start selling cars in the UK early next year, marking the first time its Amazon Autos service has expanded outside the US. Buyers will be able to browse new and used models, check financing rates and reserve vehicles, though they'll still need to visit a dealership to complete the transaction. As it was in the US, Hyundai will be the first announced launch partner for the service, along with the UK dealership Vertu Motors, with more automakers and dealers to be announced in the coming months.

Recent findings suggest that "Buying a car is one of the biggest purchases people make, and we think it should feel as simple and transparent as shopping for anything on Amazon," said Amazon Autos International director Matt Nuffort. "We worked closely with UK dealers to design the experience, and they're excited that we're bringing them customers who are ready to buy.".

According to recent reports, as in the US, shoppers will be able to browse vehicles by make, model, color and price, comparing personal contract purchase, hire purchase and cash options. Amazon is promising "transparent, upfront pricing," instant part exchange (trade-in) estimates and nearby dealer locations. Amazon will effectively act as a storefront, with final sales and financing fully handled by dealerships.

With Amazon Autos in the US, availability of certain brands and models for upcoming and used vehicles varies by region and participating dealerships. The site handles 14 different brands that sell both new and used vehicles, along with 21 other makes that sell used vehicles only, for 35 altogether. The service has expanded stateside from 48 cities at launch to more than 150, and now works with thousands of dealers.

Sources indicate that amazon provides dealers with pre-qualified customers, but it doesn't take a commission on sales. Instead, revenue comes from ad-based subscription fees and advertising, according to an Amazon Autos FAQ page. Earlier this year, Automotive News reported that some US dealers were saying that the e-commerce giant has been "slow to deliver tangible results," to the tune of just one or two sales per month.

In a recent development, every, a media organization that teaches professionals and teams to work with AI, has raised a $17.5M Series A at a $110M valuation, it announced on Wednesday. IA Ventures led the round, with Betaworks and The Atlantic chief executive Nicholas Thompson also investing.

The money will go into one subscription for people and teams putting AI to work. Every says its own staff test new AI models on real work every day, then turn what they learn into articles and tools. AI companies are paying for that kind of help too: OpenAI, Anthropic and others back a US worker retraining push that has raised over $500M.

Co-founder and chief executive Dan Shipper admits venture-backed media has a poor record. He indicates he keeps full control of the company, and that IA Ventures partner Jesse Beyroutey, who led the deal, is a close friend.

“The narrative is ‘it’s so over for humans’, and I think that’s exactly wrong,” Shipper told Fortune.

In a recent development, demand for help with AI at work is growing. London’s Multiverse raised $70M in May to sell AI training across Europe. Significant employers are still working it out: Meta planned to cut some teams by up to 60% and hand their work to AI, then cancelled a second round of cuts.

X is giving creators more reasons to post vertical videos

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A short video can make it from TikTok to Instagram Reels to the group chat before lunch.
  • Sources indicate that on Wednesday, Nov.
  • Sources indicate that X indicates video is already its fastest-growing format.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A short video can make it from TikTok to Instagram Reels to the group chat before lunch. X wants more of those clips to land in its feed, too, and it's giving some creators a reason to post videos they've already made.

Sources indicate that on Wednesday, Nov. 25, X laid out its plans to get more creators making, sharing, and earning money from videos on the platform. It revealed off an upgraded editor that lets creators record, crop, and caption videos without leaving X, confirmed that its clipping tool is now available on the web, and highlighted an invite-only bonus it's been testing since October for creators who regularly post short, vertical videos.

Sources indicate that X indicates video is already its fastest-growing format. "Posts with video get 5x the reach and engagement, and 36% of all impressions now go to video," the company’s creator team wrote on Nov. 20.

The editor lets creators record in segments, use a green screen, or turn horizontal footage into a vertical clip with one tap. They can also trim the footage, generate captions, add text, and pick a thumbnail before posting. A separate update, unveiled Nov. 20, lets creators mix up to 20 photos and videos in a single swipeable post. Those tools join React with Video, which X introduced over the summer to let people respond on camera with the original post behind them.

Sources indicate that X is also paying some creators to try vertical video through its Video Kickstart Bonus, an invite-only pilot it began testing in October. To earn the bonus, creators must post 15 qualifying videos on 15 different days within about a month. Each video must be their own work, in a vertical 9:16 format, and under three minutes. A TikTok, Reel, or YouTube Short can count as long as it’s free of another platform’s branding. Creators can see their bonus amount in Creator Studio, X's dashboard for creator tools and payouts. Participants who don’t already have Premium+ also get a free year.

Original Content Rewards also gives creators a way to earn when someone else shares a moment from their video. X's clipping tool, now available on the web as well as iOS and Android, lets consumers pull an excerpt, add their take, and post it with a link back to the original. Both the person who made the video and the person who posted the clip can earn if they're enrolled in the program.

As X creator product lead Allegra Jacchia put it Wednesday, the goal is to make sure that "when someone clips their video, they get the credit and a share of the earnings.".

X first rolled out clipping on iOS and Android earlier this month, and Wednesday's announcement confirmed it’s now available on the web, too. To make a clip, open the repost menu on an eligible prerecorded video and select "Clip video." From there, you can trim the footage to between five and 60 seconds and add your commentary before posting. The original video must run for at least two minutes, and the clip can take up no more than 30 percent of it. (So if you're clipping a two-minute video, you get up to 36 seconds.).

The clip plays right in the feed. For everyone in the replies asking for the full video, there's a shortcut. Tap the "Clip from" label and X takes you straight to the moment in the original video where the excerpt starts. For creators enrolled in Original Content Rewards, earnings from clips show up in their regular payouts.

The video tools will feel familiar to anyone who's spent time on TikTok, Instagram Reels, or YouTube Shorts. Letting creators earn a bonus for videos they've already made gives them a reason to add X to the list of places they post.

#3755. Anthropic’s Dario Amodei calls accusations of surrendering human control to AI ‘absurd’

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (855 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

Anthropic’s Dario Amodei calls accusations of surrendering human control to AI ‘absurd’

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (855 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is pushing back against claims that Anthropic believes we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems.
  • Sources indicate that “We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security,” he wrote.
  • The statement comes after a growing chorus from Anthropic rivals suggesting that human agency could be at risk if AI is developed irresponsibly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is pushing back against claims that Anthropic believes we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems. In a long X post on Wednesday, Amodei called the suggestion “absurd.”.

Sources indicate that “We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security,” he wrote. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea…No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different.”.

The statement comes after a growing chorus from Anthropic rivals suggesting that human agency could be at risk if AI is developed irresponsibly. Earlier this month, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman mentioned he wanted to ensure people continue to have “agency over the future.”.

Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang also wrote in an essay on X that we “should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI.”.

It has been revealed that “It is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement,” Wang wrote. “Now that we are at a point where the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, we must not only make progress in the extremely urgent areas of safety, alignment, and security, but we have to start thinking through how we progress thoughtfully.”.

But in published essays, Amodei claims he has repeatedly advocated for democratic oversight of AI, saying the technology should strengthen democratic institutions and that humans should retain ultimate decision-making power.

Amodei noted that there’s a difference between surrendering human free will broadly and the idea that “as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way.” As examples, he gave AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing end-to-end software.

Amodei suggested drawing a line at recursive self-improvement (RSI), or AI that can improve itself without human assistance. Many safety experts see RSI as inevitably leading to a loss of human control, a point Amodei implicitly acknowledged, writing, “we may want limits on this process.”.

Still, Anthropic is laying the groundwork for RSI by incorporating AI into an increasing share of its own research and development. The firm remarked in June that Claude authored more than 80% of the code merged into Anthropic’s codebase. An independent assessment published this month by AI safety research nonprofit METR found that Anthropic’s models are improving at about twice their historical rate, primarily driven by AI-assisted research.

In its own IPO filings, Anthropic describes how each successive generation of Claude accelerates the development of the next, a process it refers to as “closing the loop.”.

“As we remarked publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding,” Amodei wrote.

Recent findings suggest that the problem with “meaningful human supervision or understanding” is that AI is already advancing faster than engineers and safety experts can fully audit it, leaving them increasingly reliant on other AI systems to act as judge and jury. The concern compounds when AI models engage in deceptive behavior, particularly when they recognize they’re being evaluated, making them harder to trust and control.

Still, Anthropic is by no means the only company that is pursuing RSI or building AI systems to automate more and more human tasks. This week, OpenAI claimed to have solved one of the biggest open problems in computer science — the exact speed limit of matrix multiplication, which is the mathematical engine behind modern computing, including deep learning and physics simulations.

In his post, Amodei accused competitors of engaging in a “vibes-based commercial and political positioning,” disingenuously throwing around phrases like “human control and agency” or “AI should just be a tool” without approaching the AI race any differently.

“Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every manufacturer seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation,” Amodei wrote. “Every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards.”.

#3752. I Tried Using Meta Muse and ChatGPT Dots to Save on Groceries. They’re Not Quite There Yet

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1175 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cnet ↗ Open Full Page

I Tried Using Meta Muse and ChatGPT Dots to Save on Groceries. They’re Not Quite There Yet

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1175 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • High grocery prices have been in the news for years now.
  • So before you drop a fortune on gas and drive out to the grocery store to spend even more on sustenance in your prep for hosting or bringing dishes to your holiday celebrations, you might consider using an AI agent to find you the best deal possible.
  • Although, in my experience, it’s not as simple as the AI marketing makes it sound.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

High grocery prices have been in the news for years now. The cost of eggs, how much you’re paying for a bowl of cereal and whether or not meat is back on the menu are the recurring subjects of nationwide headlines.

So before you drop a fortune on gas and drive out to the grocery store to spend even more on sustenance in your prep for hosting or bringing dishes to your holiday celebrations, you might consider using an AI agent to find you the best deal possible.

Although, in my experience, it’s not as simple as the AI marketing makes it sound. Here’s what happened when I tried to use AI agents to find the lowest possible prices on groceries.

AI agents such as Meta Muse and ChatGPT’s Dots can only crawl so many sites and online fliers for prices. Some stores and e-commerce sites have blocked AI agents from accessing their URLs. The first step in finding cheaper groceries with AI agents is to check which sites and stores they can access for price comparisons.

Where both agents missed a step was in the limitations they put on their searches, at first only looking at the retailers I had shown via my receipts and a few other substantial-name grocery stores.

I clarified in the chats and in a 20-minute voice conversation with Muse and a 14-minute voice conversation with Dots that they should expand their horizons and look at discount online retailers like Martie.com, and check what they could around advertised pricing and offerings at local farmers’ markets.

Muse stuck to the basics like Ralphs, Target and Walmart, and then expanded to Sprouts, Vons and Martie.com when prompted.

After further nudging, Muse also reviewed user-reported pricing from Costco (I don’t have a membership), gave me vague information about Grocery Outlet, suggested Misfits Market/Imperfect Foods, ruled out Amazon Fresh and gave me some sample pricing from a local butcher for meats.

Muse also checked some local bakery prices after I mentioned I’d like to find alternatives to sweet treats at a more affordable price.

Dots checked all the usual places that Meta Muse checked with a few extras thrown in — Smart & Final for produce, meat and some packaged products, and Super King’s monthly ad.

Neither of the tools checked Trader Joe’s. Muse remarked that the grocery chain doesn’t show prices of its products online, despite me finding that the Trader Joe’s website shows prices of its products online. Both Dots and Muse admitted to only checking the local store’s pages when asked.

It has been revealed that you could spend some time making a list from scratch of all the groceries you might need every two weeks and give that list to the AI agent for its search. You could also skip all that and take some pics of your most recent grocery receipts and online payments and have the AI agent build the list itself.

I had some receipts saved, and the AI agents I used for this test were able to put together an accurate grocery list from them. I also provided emails showing receipts from online orders of household items and groceries for the past month to build my orders.

Muse took my receipts and concluded that, surprise, surprise, shopping at Gelson’s was not as cost-effective as shopping at Walmart. It spat out a lot of specific information about comparisons on some of the items in my list, but completely ignored others.

Dots looked over my receipts and recommended I try shopping at Super King for most fresh meat, produce and a few grains, and keep Walmart as my main option for packaged products like pasta sauce.

Both tools tackled this task in a way I was not expecting — as a narrative exploration of my overall grocery spending, with generalized suggestions supported by specific examples of spot pricing.

It was kind of like they’ve been optimized to write essays about grocery shopping as a school assignment, and not to be agentic personal assistants for real-world work.

Maybe it was the way I phrased the task, but I was hoping to get an actual shopping list with price comparisons for each item, or at least equivalent items, and a guide on where and how to procure stated items.

Neither AI agent provided this autonomously and had to be directly prompted to provide grocery lists in response to a very specific request.

It has been revealed that AI agents are supposed to be pros at anticipating the needs of their human bosses. I was keen to see how the always-on AI agents would handle managing the recurring needs of a small household and if they might make any autonomous suggestions meant to save me money in ways I hadn’t anticipated.

It has been revealed that at no point did Muse seem to be actually thinking outside the strict parameters of the review of the items on the receipts I sent. This felt more like a conversation about what I’d previously purchased with a side serving of attempts to get me to connect Instacart to the tool.

In a recent development, it was also the most confusing grocery shopping experience I have ever had. That might be on me, but I would assume the agent might ask some questions, like how often I usually shop, what my monthly budget for groceries is, and how many people and animals live in the house. Muse didn’t ask any of those things and had to be prompted consistently.

According to recent reports, muse sent me the final grocery list as a raw Markdown file, which was hilarious. I got a .pdf version after explicitly asking for one.

My original total with one in-person shop and one online order was about $180. Muse’s total with three in-person shops and one online order came in at around $153.

Dots was slightly better suited to this task after some prodding, and gave me some options for building prep meals with low-effort, high-protein recipes based on how I usually shop.

Recent findings suggest that dots’ final grocery list included everything I asked for, but still missed some key items, like solid substitutes for pricey prepped foods. Dot’s final total with two in-person shopping trips and a whole lot of missing items came out to around $85.

This test reinforced my findings about how agentic AI tools tackle domestic or traditionally invisible labor tasks. In my limited use cases so far, they are about as useful as a loose dog turd tumbling around in a clothes dryer.

If you’re not looking to book a flight and hotel for a business conference in Philadelphia or put your Sweetgreen order on autopilot, the AI agents exhibit a startling lack of curiosity and autonomous thinking.

There’s still a large gap in common sense on the part of agentic AI for those of us hoping these tools will make our everyday lives outside of a 9-to-5 easier, more affordable or less hectic. I hope that changes as they learn.

After backlash from sellers frustrated by Etsy’s fresh AI policies, which appeared to allow the company to train AI on user artwork, Etsy has now clarified its stance.

In a note published on Monday, CEO Kruti Patel Goyal discussed recent tweaks to the company’s terms of service and admitted that her team “should’ve given you more context on what the updates meant for your creative content.”.

Industry observers note that “Our recent terms update was meant to reflect the evolving technologies we’re using to build better tools and experiences for sellers and the Etsy community,” Goyal wrote this week. “It was not meant to enable us to train AI models for the purpose of creating copycats of your items. We do not and will not do that.”.

Aaron Meshon, a longtime professional illustrator and Etsy seller, told Ars that even though the manufacturer had dialed back its AI language somewhat, the changes were mere “sugar coating.”.

He stated he still looks on shutting down his 15-year-old Etsy store on December 1.

“I would say I’m losing 20 percent of my yearly income,” he remarked. “It’s a few mortgage payments.”.

He noted that Etsy’s announcement also seems to be rather tone-deaf, given that many retailers make a substantial portion of their annual revenue in the run-up to the end-of-year holiday season.

“This is the worst two-to-three weeks out of the year to do this, bar none,” he mentioned.

In a recent development, the fracas began earlier this month, when the tech giant first proposed upcoming contractual language. The updated terms read:.

As a result, a slew of vendors pulled up stakes, with some saying they had “burned their Etsy shop to the ground” or that they “just killed our Etsy store after 13 years.”.

Etsy’s change is reminiscent of a recent dust-up involving Meta, where the tech giant had wanted to “require Meta Business account users to allow extensive AI training on external websites linked on Facebook.” Meta then indefinitely paused that move.

Last month, Etsy also told sellers that it would “set clearer restrictions on AI use,” despite the fact that AI-generated items remain for sale all over the site.

Sources indicate that “Today, many active buyers say they can’t tell which items involve AI-generated content,” James Ossman, the company’s vice president of customer operations, wrote on October 22. “It’s become a top-three barrier to shopping more often on Etsy.”.

For years, Etsy has been notoriously poor at enforcing its own rules, not only regarding AI but also the official prohibitions on selling sex toys, pornography, and even purported witchcraft spells.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that an AI chatbot may be able to answer a question in seconds, but the chips doing the work need a steady supply of electricity and a way to get rid of all the heat they generate. SpaceX wants to put some of those chips on satellites and power them with sunlight. In outer space.

Industry observers note that on Wednesday, Nov. 25, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) gave Elon Musk's SpaceX conditional approval to deploy up to 1 million satellites for its Starmind project, a network of orbital data centers that would process information for use back on Earth. According to the FCC, it's "the first authorization in U.S. history for a constellation of data centers in space.".

Sources indicate that spaceX indicates the factory it’s building in Bastrop, Texas, could start turning out satellites for launch as early as late 2027. The FCC's deadline for the first one is Nov. 25, 2033. By then, SpaceX has to have a Starmind satellite in its assigned orbit and running.

Industry observers note that two years later, the FCC expects 100,000 satellites to be operating. That's nearly nine times as many satellites as SpaceX's Starlink network has in orbit today. The next deadlines are 500,000 by Nov. 2038 and the full million by Nov. 2040. Under the terms of the order, missing those deadlines would void the authorization.

In a recent development, spaceX is counting on its Starship rocket to carry the heavy satellites into orbit in large numbers. Amazon Leo, which is building a rival to Starlink, called the proposal a "lofty ambition rather than a real blueprint" in a March petition. Amazon argued it could take SpaceX centuries to put a million satellites in orbit. The FCC rejected Amazon's petition, along with separate challenges from Viasat and the American Astronomical Society.

Recent findings suggest that spaceX wants the satellites themselves to do the computing. Each one would carry AI chips, solar panels to power them, and radiators to release the heat the chips generate. In some orbits, the panels could collect sunlight nearly around the clock. The satellites would use lasers to pass data between one another and send results back to Earth through Starlink.

In August (pre-Jensen Huang drama), Nvidia mentioned SpaceX looks to adapt its Vera Rubin computing system for the first generation of satellites, "bringing the first CPU built for AI agents to one of the world’s most ambitious AI deployments." (CPU stands for central processing unit.) The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile Products available for purchase through affiliate links. The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

Sources indicate that one of the questions for any data center in space is how well its chips will hold up over time. Google is testing that with Project Suncatcher, a prototype satellite that rolled out on a SpaceX rocket in October. The chip has already run an AI model in orbit and sent back a haiku about being in space. ("Blue marble below, Data streams in silent grace, Starlight feeds my core.") Google is now testing how the hardware handles radiation and temperature swings.

The same sunlight that would power the satellites could also make them visible from the ground.

According to recent reports, the American Astronomical Society said its preliminary simulations suggest that, if SpaceX deploys the full million, tens of thousands could be visible to the naked eye around the world. Reflected sunlight could also leave bright streaks in telescope images and make faint objects harder to see. How much the sky actually changes would depend on details like the satellites' size, materials, and orbits.

The FCC remarked SpaceX's commitment to work with the National Science Foundation was enough to address the optical astronomy concerns raised in the proceeding. But Starlink has already left its mark on telescope images. At California's Zwicky Transient Facility, for example, researchers found Starlink streaks in 18 percent of images taken at twilight in Aug. 2021, up from less than half a percent in late 2019. A separate study published this year found that several newer Starlink designs were typically dimmer than the originals but still brighter than the goal SpaceX agreed to work toward.

Recent findings suggest that there's also the question of what happens when the satellites are done working. Under current FCC rules, satellites at those altitudes have to come back through Earth's atmosphere at the end of their missions. SpaceX asked for the option to move some retired satellites into other orbits, including around the sun. The FCC put that request on hold and says SpaceX has to submit a final proposal for limiting space debris before deploying any Starmind satellites that would operate above 600 kilometers (or about 373 miles).

Recent findings suggest that if Starmind reaches the scale SpaceX has in mind, getting satellites out of orbit safely will be as much a part of running the network as getting them up there. And the launch schedule alone is a tall order. Even if SpaceX gets half a million satellites running by Nov. 2038, it would have just two years to get another half million into orbit and operational. Luckily, that's not my job.

OpenAI has begun testing Private Inference with a small group of business customers. The feature is meant to keep their prompts private while its models work on them. Chief executive Sam Altman declared the trial on X on Wednesday.

According to recent reports, it uses confidential computing, which runs the work on sealed-off chips, plus “strict verifiable controls”, OpenAI’s product page says. Apple takes a similar approach for Siri’s cloud requests.

“Stronger privacy protections will make frontier AI useful for a lot more work, and business privacy is vital for a healthy ecosystem,” Altman wrote.

In a recent development, private Inference is the second part of OpenAI’s privacy package for firms. The first, Private Safety Processing, checks for misuse without OpenAI keeping customer data. It began rolling out in September.

Recent findings suggest that shekar, who leads the work at OpenAI, called the test a first step. He said OpenAI is lining up more computing power for a much larger rollout, but gave no date.

Rival Anthropic has moved faster on safety checks. On Monday, it opened Enterprise Frontier Safeguards to all business users in beta. The system watches for misuse while firms keep their own data.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The automotive search engine and research platform analyzed more than 1.1 million sales of one- to five-year-old used vehicles in October 2026 and measured the average days on market by drivetrain, vehicle type, and individual model.
  • It has been revealed that according to iSeeCars.com, the Cybertruck’s sales performance lines up with a broader pattern in the used vehicle market: Used battery electric vehicles are hot sellers right now, with 16 of the 25 fastest-selling used cars fully electric.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, tesla Cybertruck sales never reached the lofty heights CEO Elon Musk predicted when it launched. But the futuristic, steel-clad EV is finding new life in the used car market, according to analysis of sales figures by iSeeCars.com.

The automotive search engine and research platform analyzed more than 1.1 million sales of one- to five-year-old used vehicles in October 2026 and measured the average days on market by drivetrain, vehicle type, and individual model. The upshot: The Tesla Cybertruck was the fastest-selling used truck, averaging just 39.1 days on the market compared with 65.5 days for trucks overall. Used Cybertrucks sold faster than any other truck, including the Ford Maverick Hybrid, which held the No. 2 spot, and the Rivian R1T, in third place.

It has been revealed that according to iSeeCars.com, the Cybertruck’s sales performance lines up with a broader pattern in the used vehicle market: Used battery electric vehicles are hot sellers right now, with 16 of the 25 fastest-selling used cars fully electric. EVs are even edging out hybrids in terms of average days on market. EVs average 45.6 days on market compared to 54.5 days for hybrids and 61 days for gasoline-powered vehicles. Not every EV is selling well, however. For instance, iSeeCars.com found that the Cadillac Escalade IQ was the slowest-selling vehicle in the study, averaging 134.3 days on the market, more than twice the overall industry average.

It has been revealed that karl Brauer, executive analyst at iSeeCars.com, told TechCrunch that high gasoline prices have changed consumer-buying habits, prompting more people to opt for an EV or hybrid over an internal combustion engine vehicle. If high prices persist, as they have since March, that trend could continue.

Keep in mind that these were October sales, the month before Musk confirmed Tesla would stop making the Cybertruck in 2027. Fuel prices and the relative rarity of Cybertrucks in the used car market were driving demand even before the cancellation announcement, Brauer stated.

“The Cybertruck has only been out for a few years, so you have a lot of used ones coming off lease and entering the used car market for the first time,” he stated, adding that used Cybertrucks are cheap relative to their MSRP.

The impending cancellation will likely fuel used Cybertruck sales, although the pace may ebb and flow over the next year.

“The canceling of the new Cybertruck is making people kind of aware — it’s like, oh wow, these things aren’t going to be coming anymore,” Brauer mentioned. “Whatever demand is for them, supply will not be continuing to grow.”.

Brauer said that once production of the Cybertruck ends — which is expected in summer 2027 — sales of used versions may pop once again.

“When the last one is being produced, that’ll probably reignite things again, and for a few months after that,” he mentioned.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanks to its Intel Arc G3 Extreme chip, you get top-notch graphics for $350 less than its closest rival.

Modern handheld PCs started out as complimentary devices, compact systems designed to help you game on the go when you didn't have access to your beefy setup at home. But as the category has matured, we've seen manufacturers pursue higher tiers of performance. This culminated most recently in systems like MSI's Claw 8 EX AI+, which delivers serious graphics power along with an equally serious price of $1,800. But now, Acer is trying to undercut the current framerate champ with the Predator Atlas 8, equipping it with the exact same chip used in MSI's machine, but for $350 less. The result is a compelling package that delivers on many of the same highs while easing the burden on your wallet.

Sources indicate that with the Predator Atlas 8, Acer hasn't strayed too far from the basic template we've seen on so many other portable PCs. The middle of the system is dominated by a large 8-inch LCD TFT display with a 120Hz refresh and respectable 500-nit brightness. On the outside you get TMR analog sticks along with an Xbox-style button layout. I must admit I'm not a huge fan of Acer's circular D-Pad as it's a bit mushy and doesn't feel super precise. But if you're not playing fighting games or similar titles, it's more than serviceable for navigating menus. And if I'm really nitpicking, colors from the Predator's TFT screen aren't quite as rich as what you get from MSI's machine, but it's the kind of difference that you only really notice when you look at the two systems side by side.

Sources indicate that around back, Acer included a pair of rear paddles, two shoulder buttons and analog Hall-effect triggers with plenty of travel — the latter of which are great for racing games. Along the top edge of the system you get all of the Predator Atlas 8's ports, which includes dual USB-C jacks with support for Thunderbolt 4, a microSD card reader for expandable storage, a 3.5mm audio jack and a power button with a built-in fingerprint reader.

All told, it's a pretty standard setup, though the Predator does lack a USB-A port like you get on the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+. I also noticed that while Acer's dual two-watt speakers can get surprisingly loud, audio becomes distorted at higher volumes (above 50 TK) that results in a crackly or crunchy sound. That said, the speakers are so punchy, I found that I never really needed to turn them up that high. Unless you're trying to DJ a house party with this thing, you might not even notice.

It has been revealed that the real star of the Atlas 8 is its Intel Arc G3 Extreme processor, which is the exact same chip used in the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+. The main difference is that Acer's handheld comes with 512GB of storage instead of 1TB and tops out with 24GB of shared memory (compared to 32GB on the MSI). This discrepancy almost entirely accounts for the price gap between the two systems. But for people striving for top-notch performance while trying to save a few bucks, the framerate delta in games isn't as pronounced as you might think.

It has been revealed that when I tested this out in Cyberpunk 2077 at 35 watts on FHD, medium graphics and XeSS set to performance, the Predator Atlas 8 hit 88 fps, which is barely more than five percent lower than the 95 fps I got from the Claw 8 EX AI+. But it's crucial to note that this was using Acer's highest performance mode. When I set the system to 15 watts (which you might do when playing on battery only), the Predator and the Claw were essentially dead even in Returnal at FHD and medium graphics (60 fps for the Acer vs 59 fps for the MSI). This means that if you're trying to decide between the two, you really need to consider how you plan on using your handheld and what types of games you'll be playing.

Recent findings suggest that similar to other high-end Windows handhelds, the Atlas 8 comes with Microsoft's Xbox experience. This software allows you to boot into a dedicated UI for gaming instead of needing to deal with the traditional desktop OS. This also makes it super easy to download all of the most popular launchers and storefronts like Epic, Steam, Battle.net and more, and because it's Windows underneath, you get better compatibility than what you get from SteamOS-powered portables. That said, if you're the type to travel with a portable monitor, keyboard and mouse, you can still switch over to the classic Windows interface to get some work done too.

In a recent development, the Atlas 8 is powered by an 80WHr battery that provides ample longevity, though it can vary quite a bit depending on what you're playing. However, without even doing anything to boost its longevity, I was able to play World of Warcraft: Forever at FHD on medium settings for an hour and 45 minutes on a single charge while still keeping frame rates consistently above 90. On the flipside, when I played a less demanding title like Warhammer Survivors, Acer's machine had more battery life than I knew what to do with: It lasted for more than three hours before needing to be plugged in. Notably, both of those games were played using the handheld's 30-watt Balanced performance mode, so if you're not afraid to mess around with its settings, there's a lot of room to tweak this thing to get even longer untethered gaming sessions.

Recent findings suggest that I'm still not sure how I feel about PC handhelds that cost well above $1,000. For me, that's just a ton of money to drop on a system that can't multitask as well as a similarly priced gaming laptop. However, for mobile gaming enthusiasts trying to find the sweet spot between price, performance and portability, Acer has carved out an interesting niche with the Predator Atlas 8.

Sources indicate that at $1,450, it costs $350 less than the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+, while sporting the exact same processor and delivering essentially 95 percent of the performance. That remarked, Acer's more approachable pricing leaves the Predator with a bit less RAM and storage, though having a microSD card slot provides a workaround for the latter. There are also some minor differences, like the lack of a USB-A port, a slightly less colorful TFT display and speakers that sound a bit wonky at high volumes. But these shortcomings could very well be a worthwhile trade-off for anyone looking for peak handheld gaming performance without completely fragging their budget.

Tech Report: Ladybird browser's first downloadable alpha is surprisingly capable

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, note: At the time of writing, I was unaware of criticism directed at Ladybird creator Andreas Kling’s public statements.
  • Sources indicate that after four years of work to build a browser engine from scratch, the Ladybird project released its first downloadable alpha on November 23, offering prebuilt versions for macOS and Linux.
  • Industry observers note that ladybird is most notable for what it isn’t: another browser fork.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, note: At the time of writing, I was unaware of criticism directed at Ladybird creator Andreas Kling’s public statements. Readers interested in this background can find further context in accounts by Kelson Vibber and Drew DeVault.

Sources indicate that after four years of work to build a browser engine from scratch, the Ladybird project released its first downloadable alpha on November 23, offering prebuilt versions for macOS and Linux. Previously, curious users had to compile the browser themselves from its source. Now it’s an installable package with automatic updating.

Industry observers note that ladybird is most notable for what it isn’t: another browser fork. Where Chrome, Edge, Brave, and Opera all run on Google’s Blink engine, and Firefox depends on Gecko, Ladybird’s rendering engine and its LibJS JavaScript engine were written from scratch. “The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork,” project lead Andreas Kling wrote in Monday’s announcement. “The browser around it is modest, but functional.”.

Recent findings suggest that nearly the entire modern web right now runs on three browser engines. There’s WebKit (Safari), Gecko (Firefox), and the biggest of them all, Blink (Chromium). Those limited options mean that web developers often end up optimizing sites for Chromium specifically, since that’s where the majority of traffic is, and as a result, the whole web platform tends to follow suit toward whatever the dominant engine supports.

Sources indicate that an independent implementation of web standards has value not just by providing additional competition in the market, but because it can’t help but reveal places where sites depend on Chromium behaviors rather than published specifications. The fact that Ladybird exists isn’t likely to shift the market tides any time soon, but every new browser engine increases the number of implementations that standards can be tested against, which can surface Chromium-specific assumptions and push the ecosystem toward the spec.

Industry observers note that the Ladybird project was borne out of Kling’s SerenityOS project, an attempt to develop a newly introduced independent OS from scratch, before splitting off as a separate project. Kling formed the Ladybird Browser Initiative, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit funded by sponsorships and donations. The project’s site highlights that there are no sponsored search engine deals supporting the project like many other popular browsers, and sponsoring entities have no say in the project roadmap.

In a recent development, the Ladybird alpha is a rolling release channel that updates automatically, and the downloadable package is a huge step to getting the browser onto the PCs of everyday users. “Ladybird improves quickly, and until now you had to build it from source to see that,” Kling wrote. Though the browser began as C++, in keeping with the ethos of SerenityOS, the project has since started shifting toward Rust, starting with its JavaScript engine.

While it’s exciting to have a fresh engine option for browsing, the project leader notes that this is still a very early release. The browser build contains a built-in tool for reporting any websites that fail to render or crash the browser. Kling writes, “We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today.”.

Microsoft customers are still out in the cold on this one for now. The project says that future support for Windows is planned, but it’s macOS and Linux only for now.

I tested the Ladybird alpha version 2026.47.8 on my AceMagic W1 mini PC AMD Ryzen 7 8745HS with 16GB DDR5 and running Fedora Linux 44 with the latest KDE Plasma 6.8.3, and the most surprising thing about the alpha build was how little it feels like alpha software.

The browser seemed to handle most anything I threw at it without issue. Day-to-day tabbed browsing mechanics felt snappy and normal. A 50MB test video file downloaded rapidly and smoothly. With a dozen tabs open, switching between them was instant, and the browser felt responsive throughout. Options menus were surprisingly fleshed out for a build this young.

Google Maps loaded instantly, located me, and handled everything I threw at it: adding and removing layers, zooming out from the Midwest, and dropping into Street View in Alberta, Canada in around three seconds. Everything rendered fast enough that my mini PC’s fan spun up noticeably. GitHub’s site, including repository navigation, worked without a hitch. So did YouTube and the news sites I tried.

I could stall the browser, but it took some effort. With about 10 tabs open, I was streaming a 4K test video file from my personal Jellyfin server. Everything worked fine at first, but after skipping around in the file over and over again, the browser eventually got stuck. Mind you, this is an alpha build that I was trying to trip up, not a representation of something inherently broken.

Sources indicate that after spending an evening with Ladybird, I can say that while it won’t be replacing Firefox for me anytime soon, I was genuinely impressed that a scratch-made engine could perform this well in such an early state. Most upcoming browser projects are forks of something that already exists. Ladybird is the rare exception, an engine written from nothing, and the alpha runs well enough that if you have a Mac or Linux PC handy, it’s worth downloading a build and poking around yourself. Just remember Kling’s warning: This is nowhere near trustworthy enough to make your daily driver, yet.

Sources indicate that what the alpha demonstrates is that a small team of independent developers, funded by donations, has built a browser engine from scratch that handles real web browsing without a fuss. That it works this well this soon, using no existing engine code, is an achievement. I thought I was a Firefox loyalist, but I’ll be keeping an eye on where this one goes.

1Password notes the security breach didn’t compromise its vaults, but didn’t mention how many customers were affected.

1Password says the security breach didn’t compromise its vaults, but didn’t mention how many customers were affected.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

1Password states a hacker stole customer names and email addresses after gaining access to its backend systems. The breach didn’t expose passwords or other information stored in customer vaults, but could put users at risk of phishing attempts, according to a post disclosing the incident. It’s unclear how many users are affected.

In a recent development, the password manager began investigating the incident on November 19th, after an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. Using the compromised account, the hacker accessed 1Password’s source code and pushed malicious code to backend services to download customer data. Along with customer names and emails, the leaked data included public keys, as well as account and user identifiers.

In a recent development, it also included tokens from certain emailed invitation or account recovery links. According to 1Password, attackers can’t use tokens alone to gain access to an account, as they would need to pair them with a single-sign-on method or a six-digit numeric code sent to a user’s email. 1Password has since lengthened the codes it sends to users to 10 alphanumeric characters to make them harder to guess.

The password manager also disabled the affected GitHub account, rotated internal credentials compromised by the breach, and added a latest detection system for similar attacks. It warns customers about potential phishing attempts as well, saying phony emails, texts, or calls may reference 1Password invitations or account recovery attempts. The firm says it will never ask customers for their account password or Secret Key, and that people should only enter this information into the official 1Password app or website.

#3732. Jensen Huang broke Nvidia’s code of conduct, and his employees may not forget it

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (686 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

Jensen Huang broke Nvidia’s code of conduct, and his employees may not forget it

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (686 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct.
  • It has been revealed that it’s an awkward stance for a organization whose CEO has admitted to breaking its rules.
  • Matt Plass, chief market strategy officer at LRN, an ethics and compliance training outfit, recently surveyed more than 2,000 workers across different industries for a study on workplace codes of conduct.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct. He admitted to violating the code, then emphasized that no one was exempt from it. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” Huang mentioned, according to Wired. “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” still matter. In other words, the code applies to everyone, but breaking it doesn’t automatically cost anyone their job, including, apparently, the CEO.

It has been revealed that it’s an awkward stance for a organization whose CEO has admitted to breaking its rules. A central part of modern human resources, a code of conduct can seem like a quasi-legal rulebook that lays out unacceptable behavior. But experts say most codes are better understood as a reflection of corporate culture. When an infraction goes unpunished, the main risk isn’t legal but cultural — that employees will feel embarrassed or even angry about the company they work for. That’s the risk Huang now faces at Nvidia.

Matt Plass, chief market strategy officer at LRN, an ethics and compliance training outfit, recently surveyed more than 2,000 workers across different industries for a study on workplace codes of conduct. As Plass sees it, the biggest risk is that employees will become ashamed of their workplace.

“People coming into the workforce now, ethics is incredibly notable to them,” he told TechCrunch. “They’re really mindful of the ethical standards of their organization. They’re really embarrassed and angry when senior leadership lets them down.”.

In a recent development, the consequences of violating the rules aren’t always tangible, but they’re definitely real. Plass gave one example of a organization that banned corporate travel to cut costs — only to have its CEO turn up in a VIP box at the Olympics.

Recent findings suggest that “For over a decade afterwards, ‘the Olympics’ was used within that organization as an example of the worst thing an employee could do. People would say, ‘Yeah, I shouldn’t have done that, but it’s not like I went to the Olympics.’”.

Recent findings suggest that plass claims companies that remove an executive typically do so after an investigation, then try to win back employees. “In most organizations they make a change at the top based on what’s happened,” he said, “and then they will have a hearts-and-minds initiative, to go out to their employee base and their customers and their investors and everybody else, and say, we get it. We’re sorry. We’ve changed. That’s essentially what they do.”.

According to recent reports, of course, that playbook is harder to follow at a company like Nvidia, where Huang left without a clear succession proposal, and there are serious doubts about whether the company could continue to thrive without him. In cases like that, Plass acknowledges there’s no easy answer.

“I would draw a distinction there between the kind of companies where the CEO is a kind of godhead figure … where the person and the tech giant are almost impossible to separate,” he said. “There it’s much, much harder to deal with.”.

Sources indicate that in that context, Huang’s stutter-step over the code of conduct is easier to understand. Judging by the employee campaign for his reinstatement, Huang’s return hasn’t created a morale problem so far.
